title: My family
goal: Name family members, use *avere*, and master the odd rule of possessives: the article is dropped for a single family member.
bekal: name members of your close and extended family
use *mio*, *tuo*, *suo* with or without the article, as the rule requires

notes: **Age uses avere, not essere.** *Ho ventidue anni* literally means "I have twenty-two years". Saying *sono ventidue* is the most common mistake English speakers make here, and it's instantly noticeable. Italian agrees with French and Spanish on this: you have your age, you don't "are" it.
**The word anni can't be dropped.** In English "I'm twenty-two" is complete. In Italian *ho ventidue* just hangs there meaninglessly — *anni* is required.

**The odd rule of possessives.** Possessives normally take an article: *il mio libro*, *la mia casa*. But with a **single** family member, the article is dropped: *mia madre*, *mio padre*, *tua sorella*.
**In the plural, the article comes back.** *I miei fratelli*, *le mie sorelle*. So the rule is: family + singular = no article; everything else takes one.

**And as soon as something is added, it comes back too.** *La mia sorella maggiore* (my older sister) takes the article, because the noun has been described. The same goes for affectionate forms: *la mia mamma*.
**Abitare and vivere both mean "to live".** *Abitare* points more to your address, *vivere* more to your life. *Abito a Bologna* and *vivo a Bologna* are both correct and both common.
**A for cities, in for countries.** *A Bologna*, *a Giacarta*, but *in Italia*, *in Indonesia*. Learn this pair from the start; mistakes here really stand out.
**Che bella foto!** To pay a compliment: *che* + adjective + noun, with no article. *Che bel ragazzo!*, *Che buona pizza!* The pattern is simple and used constantly.

grammars.title: Avere — the verb "to have"
body: Irregular like *essere*, and used just as often. Notice the **h** in four of the forms: it's completely silent, just a spelling marker so they aren't confused with other words.
after: *Ho* is said "oh", *hai* "eye", *ha* "ah", *hanno* "AHN-noh". Without the h, they'd clash with *o* (or), *ai* (to the), *a* (to, at), *anno* (year).

*Avere* is also used for physical states: *ho fame* (I'm hungry), *ho sete* (thirsty), *ho freddo* (cold), *ho caldo* (hot), *ho sonno* (sleepy), *ho paura* (scared). All of them are "have", not "be".

grammars.title: Possessives
body: Italian possessives agree with the **thing owned**, not the owner. *Il suo libro* can mean his book or her book; what decides the form is *libro*.
after: The *loro* row is the only one that never changes — only its article adjusts.
Because the form follows the thing owned, *Marco ama la sua città* can mean Marco's city or someone else's. If you need to be clear, add *di lui* or *di lei*.

blocks.text: Watch out for *i parenti*: it means "relatives", **not** "parents". Parents are *i genitori*. It's a classic trap for English speakers.
Mixed groups always take the masculine plural: two brothers and three sisters are still *i fratelli*. That's why *Quanti fratelli hai?* actually asks about all your siblings, not just the brothers.

blocks.title: Talking about age and status
items: *Quanti anni hai?* — How old are you? (informal) / *Quanti anni ha?* (formal)
*Ho trent'anni.* — I'm thirty. Notice *trenta anni* clipped to *trent'anni*.
*Hai figli?* — Do you have children? Answer: *Sì, ho due figli.* or *No, non ho figli.*

blocks.text: Combining them is just a matter of sticking them together: *ventitré*, *trentacinque*, *sessantotto*. Two small adjustments: before *uno* and *otto*, the tens drop their last vowel — *ventuno* (not *ventiuno*), *ventotto*, *trentuno*, *quarantotto*. And a final three takes an accent: *ventitré*, *trentatré*.

items: How many brothers and sisters do you have?
I have one brother and two sisters.
